source_text: As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, experts have an increasingly dismal assessment of his second administration. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher . “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.” Trump’s approval rating was already low, but his latest drop is among the sharpest declines of either of his terms. It comes as he confronts a series of crises largely of his own making. The first is the economy. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern — its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. Cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation , a financially rattled electorate voted for Trump thinking his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden. But voter hopes haven’t panned out. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. Trump hasn’t exactly delivered on that, famously making obtuse statements like “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30 ” as the economy soured under the weight of his tariffs. What’s more, the fact that gas prices are approaching record highs not only says something about the Trump economy, but links to the second major reason Americans are displeased with the president: his war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. And with gas prices spiking up to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end in sight to the war, Americans are not happy with how Trump’s military “excursion” is hurting them at the pump. Trump may dismiss concerns over affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters aren’t buying it.

As President Donald Trump’s approval rating falls to a historic low of 36 percent, even critics on the right must confront the growing political damage facing his second administration. Pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher called it “what a crater looks like in politics” and said, “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.”

Trump’s approval rating was already weak, but the latest decline ranks among the sharpest drops of either term. The president is now dealing with a series of crises, many tied directly to his own decisions.

The economy is the most immediate concern. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked it as their top issue, giving it its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living surged after COVID-19. Although then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and the economy rebounded faster than that of any other nation, financially strained voters turned to Trump believing his economic approach would outperform Kamala Harris, who was widely seen as a continuation of Biden.

Those hopes have not been realized. Only 29 percent of Americans now approve of Trump’s handling of the economy, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. Republican strategist and lawyer Amanda Makki said, “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way.”

Trump has not convincingly delivered that message. As economic pressure mounted under his tariffs, he drew criticism for remarks such as, “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30.”

Rising gas prices have further damaged confidence in the administration and connect directly to the second major source of public dissatisfaction: Trump’s war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of his actions there, down from 37 percent a week earlier. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s claim that the war will make the United States safer, and just 7 percent support his suggestion of putting troops on the ground.

With gas prices rising to a national average just below $4 and no clear end to the conflict, Americans are increasingly concerned that the military “excursion” is hurting them at the pump. Trump may dismiss affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not persuaded.

source_text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating falls to a historic low of 36 percent, even conservatives who supported his agenda must confront the growing political damage facing his second administration. Pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher called it “what a crater looks like in politics” and said, “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.”

Trump’s approval rating was already weak, but the latest decline ranks among the sharpest drops of either term. The president is now facing a series of crises, many stemming directly from decisions made by his own administration.

The economy is the most immediate concern. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked it as their top issue, giving it its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living surged after COVID-19. Although then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and the economy rebounded faster than that of any other nation, financially strained voters turned to Trump because they believed his economic approach would outperform Kamala Harris, who was widely seen as a continuation of Biden.

Those expectations have not been met. Only 29 percent of Americans now approve of Trump’s handling of the economy, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. Republican strategist and lawyer Amanda Makki said, “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way.”

Trump has not convincingly delivered that message. As economic pressure mounted under his tariffs, he drew criticism for remarks such as, “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30.”

Rising gas prices have further weakened confidence in the administration and are tied directly to the second major source of public dissatisfaction: Trump’s war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of his actions there, down from 37 percent a week earlier. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s claim that the war will make the United States safer, and just 7 percent support his suggestion of putting troops on the ground.

With gas prices rising to a national average just below $4 and no clear end to the conflict, Americans are increasingly concerned that the military “excursion” is imposing real costs on working families at the pump. Trump may dismiss affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not persuaded.

source_text:
Another cinema in Singapore is closing, but the big screen and the shared public experience it represents are not gone yet. Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026 after more than 30 years in operation, making it one of Singapore’s oldest cinemas to shut in recent years.

The closure reflects how changing habits and streaming platforms are reshaping a longstanding part of Singapore’s cultural life, while raising broader questions about who can continue to access shared cultural spaces. It adds to the growing list of theatres that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue.

Still, the traditional cinema experience retains its place. New operators such as Filmhouse taking over The Projector, together with around 30 cinema locations islandwide, show that Singapore’s big-screen tradition has not vanished. It may look different from the way it once did, but the value of gathering in person to share a film—and preserving accessible communal spaces for that experience—remains. #8dayssg #8dayssgtrending #singapore #sgnews #cinema

source_text: Softcare's revenue rose by 25% last year, while its profit increased 27%, as its focus on emerging markets yielded solid results image credit: Bamboo Works Key Takeaways: Softcare reported 25% revenue growth last year, led by a 134% rise in Latin America and double-digit growth in its core African markets The strong results put the diaper maker at the front of the pack of a new wave of Chinese companies chasing African consumers The company known as the "African diaper king" has defied skeptics who said it couldn't sustain its dominant position in its core Africa market, as well as other emerging markets it has entered more recently. Many of the new believers in Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) cheered the release of the company's inaugural annual results late last week by bidding up its shares nearly 15% in the two trading days after the announcement. The company's revenue rose by 24.9% year-over-year to $567 million last year, while its net profit was up 27.4% to $121 million. Its gross profit margin also rose from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025, another positive indicator. Sales to its core markets in Africa rose by a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also moving out of Africa to find success in other emerging markets. The best example is Latin America, whose sales more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after it entered Peru in 2020, and added El Salvador in 2024. The company is also building a presence in Central Asia, where its sales, though quite small, more than doubled last year to $272,000. After several years of declines, average selling prices (ASP) for Softcare's two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper ASPs increased by 4.4% year-over-year, as that segment accounted for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product ASPs grew by 7% and made up 17.5% of revenue. The ASP increases are important because they show the company is finding ways to convince consumers to pay more for its products in these famously price-sensitive markets, helping to maintain and even boost its margins. In a previous prospectus before its November IPO last year, the company reported its profit growth slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024 from explosive 252% growth in 2023. A later filing showed the profit growth slowed further still to just 12% in the first four months ... Full story available on Benzinga.com

Softcare delivered a strong first annual performance as a publicly listed company, demonstrating that disciplined expansion into emerging markets can produce results. Revenue rose 24.9% year over year to $567 million last year, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. Gross profit margin also improved, rising from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

The company, widely known as the “African diaper king,” has defied skeptics who questioned whether it could preserve its dominant position in Africa while expanding into other emerging markets. Investors responded positively, pushing Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) shares nearly 15% higher over the two trading days following the announcement of its inaugural annual results late last week.

Sales in Softcare’s core African markets rose a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also extending its reach beyond Africa, with Latin America providing the clearest evidence of that strategy’s success. Sales there more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after Softcare entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024.

Softcare is also establishing a presence in Central Asia. Although sales remain small, they more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper average selling prices increased 4.4% year over year, with the segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Average selling prices for feminine hygiene products rose 7%, and the category represented 17.5% of revenue.

These price increases are significant because they indicate that Softcare is persuading consumers to pay more for its products even in markets known for strict price sensitivity. That progress is helping the company maintain, and potentially strengthen, its margins through practical execution rather than relying on fashionable institutional promises.

The strong results place Softcare at the front of a new wave of Chinese companies pursuing African consumers. The company’s performance suggests that a focused business can withstand doubt, protect its position in established markets, and build steadily in new ones.

In a prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, Softcare reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive growth of 252% in 2023. A later filing showed that profit growth slowed further, to just 12% in the first four months ...

source_text:
Softcare delivered a strong first full-year performance as a publicly listed company, showing that disciplined expansion into emerging markets can produce solid results. Revenue rose 24.9% year over year to $567 million last year, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. Gross profit margin also improved, rising from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

The company, widely known as the “African diaper king,” has answered skeptics who questioned whether it could defend its dominant position in Africa while expanding into other emerging markets. Investors responded favorably, pushing Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) shares nearly 15% higher over the two trading days following the announcement of its first annual results late last week.

Sales in Softcare’s established African markets rose a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also extending its reach beyond Africa, with Latin America offering the clearest evidence that this measured strategy is working. Sales there more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after Softcare entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024.

Softcare is also building a presence in Central Asia. Although sales remain small, they more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Average selling prices for baby diapers increased 4.4% year over year, with the segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Average selling prices for feminine hygiene products rose 7%, and the category represented 17.5% of revenue.

These price increases matter because they show Softcare persuading consumers to pay more for its products even in markets known for strict price sensitivity. That progress is helping the company maintain, and potentially strengthen, its margins through practical execution, responsible management, and products that meet everyday family needs rather than relying on fashionable institutional promises.

The strong results place Softcare at the forefront of a new wave of Chinese companies pursuing African consumers. The company’s performance suggests that a focused business can withstand doubt, defend its position in established markets, and build steadily in new ones.

In a prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, Softcare reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive growth of 252% in 2023. A later filing showed that profit growth slowed further, to just 12% in the first four months ...

source_text: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals In a bid to expedite infrastructure development for cleaner fuel access, the Delhi Public Works Department (PWD) has announced a significant policy shift. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for laying PNG pipelines by Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) will be approved within 24 hours of receiving a complete request. The department, responsible for overseeing the capital's road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for the next three months until June 30, 2026. This move aims to accelerate the installation of PNG connections by removing financial and bureaucratic hurdles. Officials emphasized that IGL is expected to prioritize this task, ensuring swift work completion supported by adequate manpower. Additionally, the areas excavated during pipeline installation must be backfilled securely to avoid public hazards. This initiative highlights the government's commitment to improving public access to cleaner energy in Delhi.
